design_detail: Prospective cohort of women in the United Kingdom recruited in pregnancy through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements asking for pregnant women who had used recreational drugs (the Drugs and Infancy Study, DAISY): 126 responded and 96 were enrolled. The 28 women who used MDMA in pregnancy or in the month before were compared with 68 who did not (32 of them had used MDMA earlier). Use was taken from interviews (62 during pregnancy and 24 after birth). Infants were seen at about 1 month (neonatal behaviour; 82 infants) and at 4 months (Bayley mental and psychomotor scores, behaviour rating, Alberta Infant Motor Scale; 87 infants) by assessors masked to exposure. Analysis by group comparison and by regression with covariates; MDMA entered as yes or no, as tablets per week, and as three groups (heavier, lighter, none).
can_establish: Whether, in a small volunteer cohort of mostly middle-class women who used recreational drugs, infants whose mothers used MDMA in the month before or during early pregnancy differ at 1 and 4 months on standard neonatal and developmental scales from infants of similar women who did not, and what the pattern of use was (most stopped in pregnancy; median 0.13 tablets a week; one woman used in the third trimester).
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused any difference: the exposed women also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, fathers' use was not asked, 22 exposed infants were seen, and the two scale differences are among many tested; development beyond 4 months, any count of congenital anomalies, effects on miscarriage or termination, exposure in the second or third trimester, or a graded dose-response against unexposed infants (the lighter-exposed infants scored above the unexposed on two scales).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers answering midwife referrals, leaflets at prenatal clinics and advertisements in pregnancy magazines that asked for pregnant women who had used recreational drugs (ecstasy, tobacco, cannabis, alcohol and cocaine were named as examples), at Case Western Reserve University and the University of East London, with approval from both universities and National Health Service ethics committees (2.1.1 Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: maternal or child HIV, moderate or severe mental retardation or severe psychiatric or medical illness in the mother, and other major medical illness in the child. Of 126 women who responded, 5 did not meet criteria and 25 did not come to the first visit (4 miscarriages, 1 depression, 2 partner's objection, 1 moved away, 3 gave no reason, 14 could not be contacted), leaving 96.
sample.demographics: Mothers mostly white (84% and 85%), married or with a partner (84% and 79%), some university education (mean 14.9 and 15.3 years), a range of incomes, average intellectual ability on two subtests; age at birth 30.3 and 28.4 years; the exposed group had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88). Infants: 71% of exposed infants were boys against 46%; gestation 40.0 against 39.5 weeks.
sample.attrition: Infants seen: 1 month 22 of 28 exposed (79%) and 60 of 68 comparison (88%); 4 months 22 of 28 (79%) and 65 of 68 (96%); reasons not given. Birth length and head circumference were available for only 31 and 10 infants (length) and 39 and 16 (head circumference) in the comparison and exposed groups.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers who knew the study was about recreational drug use in pregnancy, mostly white, middle-class and in stable relationships; the authors say participants may have had additional concerns about risk that precipitated their involvement. The comparison group is made of women who also used drugs, so it is not a drug-free group.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at interview (trained assistants; an adaptation of the Maternal Post-Partum Interview), asking for use in the lifetime, the year before conception, the month before pregnancy, trimesters 1 and 2 and trimester 3; frequency on a 0 to 7 scale and amount per occasion; average per week. Women were classed as exposed if they said they used MDMA during pregnancy or in the month before; women who had used earlier but not then (32) or never were comparison. 62 women were interviewed during pregnancy and 24 after birth (10 of the 96 are not accounted for). No biological confirmation; tablet contents unknown.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure data, not study conditions: mean tablets per week 1.61 (SD 3.11) in the month before pregnancy (Table 4; the text gives 3.2, SD 5.2, for those who used MDMA during pregnancy), 0.82 (1.58) in the first trimester, 0.08 (0.38) in the second and 0.006 (0.03) in the third; mean total 25 tablets (SD 43.7, range 0.45 to 180) over pregnancy and the month before; median 0.13 tablets a week over pregnancy (Table 2; the text gives 0.14); lifetime average 171 times (range 6 to 936) among the women who had used before and continued in pregnancy, typically about 3 tablets (range 1 to 8) per occasion.
exposure.polysubstance: Common: women who used MDMA in pregnancy more often also used cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis (82% against 54%), tobacco (86% against 62%), amphetamine (18% against 3%), mushrooms (14% against 0), LSD (11% against 0), ketamine (7% against 0) and slightly more alcohol (96% against 91% of women; 9.1 against 6.6 units a week); the comparison women also used several drugs.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Most women stopped MDMA in pregnancy (use fell from the month before to the second trimester); only one used in the third trimester.

comparison.controls: 68 pregnant women recruited the same way who had not used MDMA in pregnancy or the month before (polydrug or non-drug-using; 32 had used it earlier).
comparison.matching: None; the groups were similar in age, education, income, intelligence subtests and ethnicity, but differed in parity and in other drugs. Covariates were retained in regressions if related to the outcome and to MDMA status at P<.20 and significant on entry (P<.10) or if they changed the MDMA coefficient by more than 10%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Fathers' drug use was not asked; maternal weight gain was not available; postnatal care, feeding and later drug use are not reported; genetic testing was done only for one infant.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group were also drug-using women, but with less cocaine, cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine, LSD and ketamine.

outcomes.instruments: NICU Network Neurobehavioral Scale (NNNS) at about 1 month corrected age (13 summary scores); at 4 months the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (Mental Development Index, Psychomotor Development Index), the Bayley Behavior Rating Scale (attention/arousal and motor quality factors) and the Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS; percentile rank and below the 10th percentile as at risk); birth data from hospital records.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard, normed instruments; NNNS coefficient alpha 0.56 to 0.82 for the summary scores; AIMS normed on 2,202 infants; habituation on the NNNS was not analysed because too few infants were asleep at the start.
outcomes.operationalization: Group comparisons by chi-square, Fisher exact, t and Wilcoxon tests; regressions (ordinary least squares, Poisson, negative binomial, logistic) with MDMA as yes or no, as average tablets per week over pregnancy, and as heavier, lighter or none (analysis of variance, with post hoc comparisons only when the overall P was below .10); heavier and lighter by a median split (0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; about 13 NNNS scores, 2 Bayley indices, 2 behaviour-rating factors, the AIMS rank and a below-10th-percentile cut-off, 8 birth measures, in unadjusted and adjusted models, with P<.05 as the threshold and P<.10 used to open further analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The NNNS examiner and the Bayley and AIMS assessors were masked to infant drug exposure; the interviewers who asked about use were not.

analysis.effect_sizes: Birth: boys 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), chi-square 5.32, P=0.02; odds ratio of a male birth after adjusting for other drug differences 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2, P<.02; the crude odds ratio from the Table 5 counts is 3.0, CI 1.2 to 7.7 (editors' calculation)); gestation 40.0 against 39.5 weeks; birth weight 3537 (SD 500) against 3344 (511) g (P=0.15, adjusted for sex); preterm 1 of 28 against 1 of 68; one exposed infant had Townes-Brocks syndrome (a spontaneous SALL1 mutation, per the authors). NNNS at 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison): no difference in any mean score (e.g., lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22; excitability 1.64 against 2.35, P=.15); trends in the score distributions (lethargy 91% against 73%, hypertonicity 9% against 27%, both P<.069). 4 months (22 against 65): Bayley mental index 99.1 against 98.6 (P=.80), psychomotor index 96.5 against 94.3 (P=.40), attention/arousal 71.2 against 70.9, motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009; AIMS percentile 50.4 against 45.8 (P=.51), below the 10th percentile 14% in both groups. After adjusting for alcohol exposure, MDMA still predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.21, P<.05); tablets per week over pregnancy predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.24, P<.042). Three groups at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (F 3.6, P<.04); AIMS percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (F 3.8, P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (F 2.6, P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18). Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005); higher cannabis exposure predicted poorer attention (beta -.28) and regulation (beta -.27) at 1 month (both P<.02).
analysis.covariates: Infant age at testing, maternal demographic and infant birth variables, maternal use of other drugs in pregnancy and maternal psychological distress were considered; the one adjustment named for the motor-quality result is average alcohol exposure.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the authors say the motor findings were predictable from the animal literature and the sex-ratio finding was unexpected.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the motor-quality difference, a dose-response and lower milestone attainment, but not the null results for the Bayley psychomotor index, the AIMS percentile and the below-10th-percentile rate in the group comparison. The three-group analyses were opened by an overall P<.10 and, for AIMS, rest on the heavier group alone being lower while the lighter group was above the unexposed. The sex-ratio difference was found after the fact.
analysis.power: The authors state that with alpha 0.05 and power 0.80 the sample could detect moderate effect sizes with up to four predictors in a regression; 28 exposed women (22 infants at follow-up), no calculation shown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 1 month no mean score differed (two non-significant shifts in the spread of scores pointed to more lethargic and less hypertonic behavior), and on the cognitive and general motor scores at 4 months, infants of women who used MDMA in the month before or during early pregnancy did not differ from comparison infants. The group difference at 4 months was a lower observer-rated motor quality score (58.9 against 74.1), which remained after adjusting for alcohol; on the AIMS the heavier-exposed infants scored lower than the lighter-exposed, while the lighter-exposed scored above the unexposed. More boys were born to the exposed women (71% against 46%). The exposed women also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, and the differences are among many tested in small groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say the findings suggest risk to the developing infant, with poorer motor quality, lower milestone attainment and a dose-response relationship, and that more male births and a rare genetic syndrome were found. The Introduction describes the 1999 letter on 136 exposed pregnancies as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk of malformations and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter prints neither figure and makes no such adjustment (the Discussion's 15.4% 'increased risk' echoes the letter's own summary). The authors themselves say they cannot establish whether the sex ratio is caused by MDMA and that the syndrome, a spontaneous mutation, cannot be attributed to the drug.

timeline.event: Case series of 136 exposed pregnancies from a UK teratology service, without a comparison group, reporting 12 anomalies among 78 live births and no effect on sex ratio

This cohort (online 3 March 2012), described by its authors as the first prospective study of MDMA-using women identified in pregnancy; no outcome measure is shared with the 1999 letter except a sex-ratio statement that points the other way

replication.where_it_stands: Not repeated in any study read here. The authors call for continued follow-up of the cohort to see whether the early motor differences persist or resolve; no later paper is in the library's reference list for this question.

funding.funder: Grant DA14910-05 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, US National Institutes of Health (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Investigators at Case Western Reserve University, the University of East London and Swansea University; the same group reported the cohort's other early findings (Moore et al., cited).

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective cohort recruited before or in early pregnancy with biological confirmation of exposure (for example hair or meconium), a comparison group handled so that cocaine, alcohol, cannabis and tobacco are dealt with, fathers' use recorded, blinded standard assessments at several ages up to school age, systematic recording of major malformations by a standard code, and outcomes named in advance with correction for the number tested.

domains.note: The exposed women used much more cocaine (71% against 16%), cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine and other drugs and slightly more alcohol; fathers' use and maternal weight gain are unknown; 22 exposed infants with several covariates; alcohol, which was adjusted for, predicted motor quality more strongly than MDMA (beta -.36 against -.21).

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-report with no biological check, 24 of 86 interviews after birth, 10 women with no stated timing, unknown tablet contents; exposure includes the month before pregnancy; the authors argue the dose-response suggests the reports are valid.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected volunteers answering advertisements for women who used recreational drugs; mostly white and middle-class; 25 of 126 responders did not attend a first visit.
Postnatal environment, breastfeeding and later maternal drug use, which could affect 4-month motor scores, are not reported.
Follow-up differed by group (exposed 79% at both visits; comparison 88% at 1 month and 96% at 4 months), with no reasons; birth length and head circumference exist for few infants.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Standardized, normed scales given by assessors masked to exposure.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Many outcomes in unadjusted and adjusted models with no correction; the abstract features the significant motor-quality, dose-response and sex-ratio results and omits the null psychomotor and AIMS group comparisons; three-group analyses opened at P<.10.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, self-selected cohort with a comparison group that differs in other drug use, self-reported exposure, differential follow-up and many uncorrected tests. The source can be cited for what was found in 22 exposed infants (no difference at 1 month or on the Bayley scores and AIMS rank at 4 months, a lower observer-rated motor quality at 4 months that persisted after adjustment for alcohol, more male births) and for the exposure pattern (low average use that mostly stopped in pregnancy); it cannot be cited for a causal effect of MDMA, for a dose-response against unexposed infants, or for any figure about malformations.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment of pregnant women who had used recreational drugs through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements; 126 responded, 5 did not meet criteria, 25 did not come to the first visit, 96 enrolled; 82 infants were seen at 1 month and 87 at 4 months.

Exposure from interviews (62 women during pregnancy, 24 after birth); women counted as exposed if they said they used MDMA in pregnancy or the month before; 32 women who had used earlier but not then, and women who had never used, formed the comparison group; 28 exposed and 68 comparison.
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2 Measures of MDMA Exposure and Covariates, 1st paragraph; 2.1.2.1 Prenatal Levels of Drug Exposure, 1st paragraph; 2.1.4 Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph; Abstract, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Use pattern: mean tablets per week 1.61 in the month before pregnancy (Table 4; 3.2 in the text for those who used MDMA during pregnancy), 0.82 in the first trimester, 0.08 in the second, 0.006 in the third; one woman used in the third trimester; mean total 25 tablets (range 0.45 to 180); the heavier (13) and lighter (15) groups were split at a median of 0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy and differed mainly in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets, P<.007; first trimester 1.6 against 0.12, P<.12).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 3rd to 7th paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Women who used MDMA had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88) and higher drug-problem scores (DAST 7.7 against 4.6); they used more cocaine (71% against 16%), cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine, mushrooms, LSD and ketamine in pregnancy and slightly more alcohol.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Birth outcomes did not differ in gestation, birth weight, prematurity, length or head circumference (the last two with missing data); exposed infants were more often boys (71% against 46%; adjusted odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 8.2); one exposed infant had Townes-Brocks syndrome (spontaneous SALL1 mutation), and results did not change without him.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5

key_findings.finding: At 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison) no mean NNNS score differed; non-significant trends for more lethargy (91% against 73%) and less hypertonicity (9% against 27%), both P<.069.

At 4 months (22 exposed, 65 comparison) no difference on the Bayley mental index (99.1 against 98.6), psychomotor index (96.5 against 94.3), attention/arousal factor or AIMS percentile (50.4 against 45.8; below the 10th percentile 14% in both); motor quality factor lower in exposed infants (58.9 against 74.1, P=.009), still significant after controlling for alcohol (beta -.21, P<.05) and predicted by tablets per week (beta -.24, P<.042).

Three-group comparison at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (P<.04); AIMS percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18). Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005) and higher cannabis exposure poorer attention and regulation at 1 month.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 2nd paragraph; Table 8; 3.5 Other Drug Effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: voluntary enrolment, self-report that may be unreliable, exposure almost entirely in the first trimester, small exposed sample, fathers not interviewed; they say the cohort had fewer confounders than most recreational drug exposure studies. They conclude the findings suggest risk to the developing child and warrant follow-up, and describe the 1999 letter as finding a 15.4% increased risk.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph (the 1999 letter); 11th paragraph (limitations); 12th paragraph (conclusion); 1. Introduction, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says exposed infants had 'poorer motor quality and lower milestone attainment at 4 months, with a dose-response relationship'. In the group comparison the Bayley psychomotor index (96.5 against 94.3) and the AIMS percentile (50.4 against 45.8; 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups) did not differ; only the motor-quality rating differed (58.9 against 74.1). The lower AIMS scores rest on the heavier-exposed infants alone: the lighter-exposed infants scored above the unexposed (65.7 against 45.9) and the heavier below (35.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: A graded dose-response against unexposed infants is not shown; the milestone result is a difference between two small exposed subgroups (about 11 infants each), and the finding on motor quality is one rated scale among many.

reporting_issues.issue: The heavier and lighter groups were split at a median of 0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy but differ mainly in use in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets a week, P<.007), not in the first trimester (1.6 against 0.12, P<.12) or the second (P>.20).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'dose' that separates the groups is largely pre-conception use, so the dose-response is not clearly a dose during pregnancy.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the 1999 letter on 136 exposed pregnancies as showing a 4 to 7 times higher risk of malformations, and, after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies, a two-fold risk; the Discussion calls its 15.4% an 'increased risk', which echoes the letter's own summary. The letter reports a proportion (12 of 78 live births) compared informally with an unreferenced 2 to 3% (a ratio of about 5 to 8 by the editors' arithmetic), with no multiples printed, no adjusted analysis and no comparison group. The same paper also says in its second Introduction paragraph that no prospective studies of prenatal MDMA exposure exist, and in the ninth Discussion paragraph calls the 1999 series the only prior prospective follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 4 to 7 times and two-fold figures are not findings of the 1999 letter and should not be repeated from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The more-male-births finding (71% against 46%) was unexpected and arose among many comparisons in a small group; the 1999 letter this paper cites reported no effect on the sex ratio; the explanations offered (hormones, heat, other toxins) are speculation.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single unexpected comparison, with a wide interval (odds ratio 3.2, 1.2 to 8.2); it is not a replicated finding and points the other way in the earlier letter.

reporting_issues.issue: The 10th paragraph of the Discussion appears garbled (it runs a statement about the paternal origin of SALL1 mutations into a sentence about fathers' exposure and a statement that the infant 'had the exposure to environmental toxins'), and cites an autism and paternal-age twin study (Lundstrom et al., 2010) in support.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reasoning about the genetic syndrome cannot be followed; the authors' own conclusion is that it cannot be attributed to the mother's drug use.

reporting_issues.issue: Interview timing is stated for 86 of 96 women (62 during pregnancy, 24 after birth), with 10 unaccounted for; the pre-pregnancy mean of 3.2 tablets a week in the text (for those who used MDMA during pregnancy) differs from 1.61 in Table 4 (the 28 exposed women) without the denominators being reconciled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Recall after birth may differ from reports during pregnancy; the exposure figures cannot be compared across the text and the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed statistics that do not match: the drug-problem (DAST) comparison is printed with t = -3.09 and P = 0.03, whereas that t value corresponds to about P = 0.003 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Likely a dropped zero; no effect on the conclusions.
